content: The September 2015 guidelines on when to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) and the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV were developed as part of the World Health Organization's (WHO) consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for treating and preventing HIV infection. These guidelines were intended to be incorporated into the updated WHO recommendations published in 2016. The document emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material do not reflect any legal or political opinions by WHO regarding the status of countries, territories, or boundaries. Additionally, the mention of specific companies or products does not imply endorsement by WHO over others of a similar nature. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information provided, but the material is distributed without any warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The guidelines define key terms and populations to ensure consistency. HIV refers to the human immunodeficiency virus, with HIV-1 being the predominant type globally. Age groups are categorized as follows: adults (over 19 years), adolescents (10–19 years), children (under 10 years), and infants (under one year). Serodiscordant couples are defined as partnerships where one individual is HIV-positive and the other is HIV-negative. Key populations disproportionately affected by HIV include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, and people in prisons or closed settings. Vulnerable populations, such as adolescent girls in sub-Saharan Africa, orphans, people with disabilities, and migrant workers, may also face barriers to accessing HIV prevention and treatment. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) involves the lifelong use of a combination of three or more antiretroviral (ARV) drugs to treat HIV infection. ARV drugs are also used for HIV prevention, including preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), reducing transmission in serodiscordant couples, and preventing HIV acquisition through post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Viral suppression refers to reducing the viral load to undetectable levels, while viral failure indicates the inability to achieve or maintain suppression below a specific threshold (e.g., 1,000 copies/ml). Universal access to ART is defined as achieving high levels of access (80% or more of the eligible population) that are affordable and accessible, though not necessarily 100% coverage. The guidelines also address approaches to PMTCT, recommending either ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding for women not otherwise eligible for ART (Option B) or lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count (Option B+). The continuum of HIV services includes prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and support for individuals at risk of or living with HIV and their families. This encompasses combination HIV prevention strategies, testing, linkage to care, management of opportunistic infections, ART initiation and monitoring, and palliative care. A public health approach aims to address the collective health needs of populations by ensuring broad access to high-quality services through simplified and standardized methods, balancing the best standards of care with feasibility in resource-limited settings. PrEP involves the use of ARV drugs by HIV-negative individuals before potential exposure to prevent HIV acquisition. Substantial risk of HIV infection is defined as an incidence rate greater than 3% in the absence of PrEP, making its provision cost-effective. Combination HIV prevention integrates behavioral, biomedical, and structural strategies to maximize the impact on reducing HIV transmission and acquisition. The guidelines were developed with contributions from various experts, organizations, and community groups. WHO acknowledges the input of external contributors, systematic reviewers, modelers, and community consultations. The guideline development process was coordinated by WHO staff and consultants, with oversight from the Department of HIV/AIDS and other relevant departments. Special thanks are extended to the WHO Guideline Review Committee and its Secretariat for their support in editing and publishing the guidelines.
